target: AG1’s claim that classroom dissection is ethically acceptable because the animals are already dead or are meat-industry byproducts.
objection: Most dissection specimens are not simply leftover dead animals; AG2 argues that roughly 99% are caught in the wild, so the supply chain still involves live capture and inhumane treatment rather than mere repurposing of waste.

target: AG1’s implication that dissection is educationally necessary or uniquely valuable for biology and medical training.
objection: AG2 argues that school biology and medical training do not require animal dissection, citing that AP Biology and NGSS do not require it and that U.S. and Canadian medical schools do not use animals for physician training, so the same educational goals can be met without dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that real animal dissection teaches better than alternatives.
objection: AG2 contends that synthetic models and computer simulations teach anatomy equally well or better than dead animals, so dissection is unnecessary for achieving the same learning outcomes.

target: AG2’s claim that wildlife capture and biodiversity loss are inherent to school dissection.
objection: AG1 objects that if schools use appropriately sourced dead animals or byproducts, dissection does not require killing or capturing live animals for the lesson, so the biodiversity-harm argument does not apply in that case.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives teach as well as real dissection.
objection: AG1 argues that synthetic models and computer simulations are simplified and standardized, and they do not reproduce the tactile properties or anatomical variability of real tissues, so they generally provide less embodied anatomical learning than real specimens.

target: AG2’s inference from the lack of medical-school use or curriculum requirements to the conclusion that school biology goals can be met without dissection.
objection: AG1 says this inference is not well-founded because physician-training objectives differ from school biology objectives, so the absence of dissection in medical training does not show that school biology can achieve its goals without it.

target: AG2’s environmental-harm/biodiversity argument based on wild-caught specimens.
objection: AG1 claims that most dissection specimens are already deceased and that fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts, so most school dissection is not plausibly supplied by wild capture and therefore does not meaningfully drive local population declines or biodiversity loss.

target: AG2’s broader claim that animal dissection is harmful because it uses animals that could be left unused or disposed of.
objection: AG1 argues that using already-deceased or byproduct animals for education is a productive and worthwhile use of material that would otherwise be discarded, not an additional harm.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection supply is typically wild-caught and therefore inherently harmful.
objection: AG1 says the vast majority of school dissection specimens are already dead byproducts from industry, so they are not mostly live wild animals when they reach schools.

target: AG2’s claim that permitting dissection necessarily causes animal and biodiversity harm through live capture.
objection: AG1 argues that if specimens are already dead byproducts destined for landfills, then dissection repurposes waste rather than causing new animal deaths or wild capture, and therefore imposes little or no incremental animal harm.

target: AG1’s claim that byproduct-based dissection avoids the biodiversity harms AG2 described.
objection: AG2 responds that typical school dissection still relies on wild-caught supply chains, so the harm AG1 says is absent is actually present in practice.

target: AG1’s claim that because many specimens are byproducts, schools are not contributing to animal harm.
objection: AG2 argues that the supply chain itself is inhumane, so even if some specimens are dead byproducts, the underlying dissection system still causes ethical harm.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is justified because it supports educational goals.
objection: AG2 replies that because alternatives can meet the same school biology goals, dissection is not justified even if it has some educational value.

target: AG1’s claim that the harms are absent when schools use dead/byproduct specimens.
objection: AG2 argues that the biodiversity-harm pathway is still present in typical school dissection because the specimens are usually wild-caught, not merely discarded byproducts.

target: AG1’s claim that appropriate sourcing removes the core harms.
objection: AG2 says that even if schools try to use dead/byproduct specimens, the overall system remains built on inhumane supply chains, so the core harms are not removed.

target: AG1’s claim that real animal dissection is educationally valuable enough to justify allowing it.
objection: AG2 counters that AP Biology and NGSS do not require dissection and that alternatives can teach as well or better, so the educational justification fails.

target: AG1’s claim that byproduct sourcing avoids inhumane and environmental harm.
objection: AG2 argues that avoiding wild capture does not eliminate the inhumane or environmentally harmful aspects of the specimen supply chain, so the harms remain even with dead/byproduct sourcing.

target: AG1’s claim that students should be allowed to dissect if specimens are appropriately sourced.
objection: AG2 says schools should still not permit dissection because the supply chain is inhumane and environmentally harmful, even when the animals are described as dead byproducts.

target: AG2’s claim that byproduct-based school dissection is inhumane because it requires live capture or killing for the lesson.
objection: AG1 responds that appropriately sourced dead/byproduct specimens avoid those inhumane aspects because schools do not need to kill or capture animals specifically for the lesson.

target: AG2’s claim that permitting dissection is ethically wrong because of the specimen supply chain.
objection: AG1 argues that using animals already destined for disposal is a productive use and therefore makes dissection ethically permissible and worthwhile when appropriately sourced.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives make dissection unnecessary.
objection: AG1 says real specimens provide distinctive educational value—hands-on anatomy, fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, critical thinking, and motivation—that alternatives do not typically match.

target: AG1’s claim that permitting dissection does not meaningfully increase harm because specimens are repurposed byproducts.
objection: AG2 argues that if schools permit dissection, they must repeatedly buy specimens, which increases upstream demand rather than merely using a fixed waste stream.

target: AG1’s claim that byproduct sourcing avoids harm.
objection: AG2 contends that higher demand for specimens would increase inhumane treatment of animals and environmental harm, so even byproduct-labeled supply chains remain harmful.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection should be allowed under appropriate sourcing.
objection: AG2 concludes that because increased demand still drives harmful procurement, schools should not permit dissection and should instead use alternatives.

target: AG2’s claim that permitting dissection increases upstream killing or capture of animals.
objection: AG1 argues that meat-industry byproducts are created by normal processing, not by school demand, so using them for dissection mainly repurposes existing material rather than increasing slaughter or capture.

target: AG2’s claim that permitting dissection meaningfully increases inhumane and environmental harms.
objection: AG1 says that if schools use appropriately sourced byproducts rather than newly captured animals, permitting dissection does not meaningfully increase those harms beyond what already occurs in the industry.

target: AG1’s claim that the absence of clearly established wild-capture supply means the harms are not clearly present.
objection: AG2 counters that typical dissection supply chains do involve newly captured wild animals, so the live-capture harm is in fact present.

target: AG1’s assumption that school specimens are obtained from a harmless existing byproduct stream rather than through live capture.
objection: AG2 argues that if supply chains typically require newly capturing animals, then schools are still obtaining specimens through live capture and later killing/preservation for the lesson.

target: AG2’s integrated claim that school dissection is unjustified because it is inherently harmful and unnecessary.
objection: AG1 responds that when schools use appropriately sourced dead/byproduct specimens, the animals were already dead through industry processes, the wild-capture harm is largely absent, and dissection still provides substantial educational value, so the integrated harms-and-necessity objection does not hold for that case.
